Implement setup, step, save, load and teardown in one script so a relaunch resumes from committed state instead of restarting.
Capture the launch configuration and environment needed to tell a changed setup apart from a broken resume.
units.why: Distributed runs multiply every unspecified choice: one missing flag or untracked code change becomes a different experiment on every rank. A written run contract makes resume and blame possible before any parallelism is added.

study.title: Reproducible environment capture
study.locator: `enforce_reproducibility`: seed handling, `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG` set before CUDA init, `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`, `cudnn.benchmark=False`; Reproduce env: `modules.txt`, `env.txt`, `pip freeze`, `git diff` of local installs

focus: The run identity is code version, dataset version, config, seeds, and hardware and software versions together. Logging `os.environ` and args, as the Lambda script does, starts the identity but `pip freeze` and the dataset version complete it.

`state.json` carries `epoch`, `global_step`, `epoch_step` and `running_loss` beside the three state dicts. Resume restores all of them and skips finished batches; loading weights alone restarts the schedule midstream.

Process-global flags are environment, not model config. The installed default is `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32` False with `torch.get_float32_matmul_precision` returning `highest`; record both in the manifest.
Teardown belongs to the contract: workers shut down, barriers complete, and only committed checkpoints are read back.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write a loop that saves model, optimizer, scheduler and a position record every N steps, stops mid-epoch, and relaunches to the same loss trajectory. State which files must exist before the resumed run may continue.
traps: Treating the random seed as the full identity. Seeding alone still leaves algorithm choice and data position unspecified.
Reading a checkpoint written by different code or config and calling the mismatch a resume bug. Reject resume under a changed configuration instead.
Saving only `model.state_dict`. Optimizer, scheduler and data position are state too; without them the trajectory diverges after resume.

selfTest.q: A resumed run reproduces the loss values but the learning rate schedule looks shifted by half an epoch. Which state was likely not restored?
selfTest.a: The scheduler state and the position record (`epoch_step` or `global_step`). Weights plus optimizer without scheduler and position restart the schedule at the wrong point.

selfTest.q: Why is logging `os.environ` and parsed args insufficient as a run identity?
selfTest.a: It misses code version, dataset version, installed package versions and process-global flags. Two runs can share env and args yet differ in code, data or library behavior.

selfTest.q: Where must `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG` be set, and why?
selfTest.a: Before the CUDA context is created, ahead of the first CUDA call. Set later it is silently ignored and matmul algorithm choice stays nondeterministic.

selfTest.q: A crash leaves new weight files but no new `state.json`. Should the resumed run load the new weights?
selfTest.a: No. Only a committed checkpoint with its position record is readable. Rebuild or discard the uncommitted shards first.

units.title: Dataset manifests, document-to-batch lineage and deterministic sampler position
outcomes: Implement a restartable sharded sampler with deterministic shuffle, disjoint coverage and a stated padding or drop policy.
Trace any batch back to document IDs and a manifest version, and serialize sampler position as epoch plus RNG state.
Diagnose duplicate or omitted samples and seed collisions across ranks and loader workers.
units.why: Data order is optimizer input: a duplicated shard or a reshuffle on resume silently trains a different model. Lineage plus sampler position makes every example accountable before ranks are added.

next.note: Count the batches the sampler yields.
Prove resume restores the exact example sequence.

study.locator: Data Loading Order and Sampler; Single- and Multi-process Data Loading with Randomness in multi-process data loading; `DistributedSampler` entry: `set_epoch`, `seed`, `drop_last` head padding, `len` reporting the per-rank count
study.depth: Read the sampler contract, not the whole loader reference. Note that `DistributedSampler` has no `state_dict`; position is the epoch integer plus the loop-owned RNG state.

study.locator: RNG save and restore (`rng.pt` with torch, NumPy and Python states), `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`, seeded `Generator` with `_seed_worker`; related-topics `optimizing-data-loading` README for `num_workers`, `prefetch_factor` and the rank-wait timer

study.title: Deterministic seeding and worker discipline
study.locator: `enforce_reproducibility(seed)`: seeds for `random`, NumPy, torch and CUDA, with the warning that `np.random.default_rng` objects built in `Dataset.__init__` are copied identically into every worker

focus: Sampler position is an epoch integer owned by the training loop plus dataset version and RNG state. Call `set_epoch(n)` every epoch or every rank replays the same order.

With `drop_last=False` an uneven split pads with head indices: 10 items over 3 ranks yield per-rank rows \([0, 3, 6, 9]\), \([1, 4, 7, 0]\) and \([2, 5, 8, 1]\). Padding duplicates examples, so token and sample counts must use the manifest, not the batch count.

Main-process shuffling assigns indices to loader workers, but an RNG object created in `Dataset.__init__` is fork-copied identically into each worker. Seed inside the worker from `torch.utils.data.get_worker_info().seed` instead.

Document-to-batch lineage means each batch element records its document ID, shard and position. A manifest fixes ordered shard paths, checksums, counts and recipe version; resume under a changed manifest is rejected.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, build a 10-item dataset with a 3-way sampler, print the per-rank index rows with `drop_last` True and False, and show that `set_epoch(0)` and `set_epoch(1)` give different orders while re-setting the same epoch reproduces them. Save and restore the epoch plus RNG state mid-epoch and continue the identical sequence.
traps: Calling `DistributedSampler.state_dict`. It does not exist; resume restores the epoch integer and the loop-owned RNG and worker state.
Assuming padding is free. Padded head items are real repeated examples that inflate token counts unless the loss denominator excludes them.
Seeding only the main process. Since PyTorch 1.9 each worker gets `base_seed + worker_id` for torch, but other libraries and prebuilt RNG objects still duplicate draws across workers.

selfTest.q: Ten items, 3 replicas, `shuffle=False`, `drop_last=False`. Which indices does rank 1 yield?
selfTest.a: \([1, 4, 7, 0]\). Each rank takes every third index and rank 1 pads with head index 0 to reach length 4.

selfTest.q: What must be saved to resume a shuffled sampler exactly?
selfTest.a: The epoch integer passed to `set_epoch`, the dataset and recipe version, and the RNG state feeding shuffle and workers. The sampler object itself holds no serializable position.

selfTest.q: Two loader workers produce identical augmentations. What is the likely cause on a current PyTorch?
selfTest.a: An RNG object created in `Dataset.__init__` was copied identically into both workers. Build or reseed the generator per worker from the worker seed.

selfTest.q: Why must resume be rejected when the manifest changed?
selfTest.a: Shard order, counts or recipe changes remap positions to different documents. Continuing from the old cursor silently duplicates some examples and omits others.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: deterministic sampler with disjoint-coverage tests, padding and drop policy, document-to-batch lineage, and interrupted versus uninterrupted record-ID equivalence.
units.stopWhen: Your sampler prints disjoint per-rank rows for both padding policies, and a mid-epoch save and restore continues the identical example sequence.

fit.note: Coverage failed for sampler position and worker randomness in the pool; the official DataLoader and Sampler reference fills that gap beside the Lambda determinism notes and the Stas seeding checklist.

units.title: Microbatches, accumulation, global batch, token accounting and update semantics
outcomes: Derive global batch and token counts from microbatch size, accumulation steps, packing and data-parallel degree.
Implement accumulation with correct mean weighting over uneven microbatches and one optimizer step per global batch.
Explain when accumulation matches a large batch and which padding and zeroing choices break the match.
units.why: The global batch sets gradient noise and learning-rate scaling, while the microbatch sets memory. Confusing the two changes the optimized objective without changing any config name.

next.note: Extend the batch equation with workers and `no_sync`.
See which states the single optimizer step updates.

study.title: Gradient accumulation and the batch equation
study.locator: Gradient accumulation through Revisiting global batch size: microbatch size, accumulation steps and \(gbs = mbs \times grad\_acc \times dp\); the note that accumulation keeps separate gradient buffers alive across the step

study.title: Accumulation and effective batch size
study.locator: Effective batch as `batch * accum_steps` with `backward` each step and `step` only when `i % accum == 0`; related-topics `effective-batch-size-and-lr` README for linear versus square-root learning-rate scaling with batch size

study.title: Capacity levers: accumulation and checkpointing
study.locator: Model Training, Pipeline Optimizations: gradient accumulation and activation checkpointing as the capacity responses when a batch does not fit

focus: Global batch is \(gbs = mbs \times grad\_acc \times dp\), with tokens \(gbs \times seq\). In LLM reports the batch is quoted in tokens so the count survives a sequence-length change.

Uneven microbatches need size-weighted averaging. With per-microbatch mean gradients \(g_1 = [1, -1]\) over 2 examples and \(g_2 = [-2, -2]\) over 1, the full-batch gradient is \([0, -1.33]\); averaging the two means gives the wrong \([-0.5, -1.5]\).

Accumulation holds gradient buffers across micro-steps, so peak memory differs from a single large batch even when the update matches. The optimizer steps once per global batch, then gradients are cleared.
Padding and packing change the denominator. Padded positions and cross-document transitions excluded from the loss must not count as tokens in the batch.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the update for two microbatches of sizes 2 and 1 with the gradients above, showing the size-weighted mean and one SGD step. Then implement accumulation over uneven microbatches and match it against a single full-batch step to 1e-5.
traps: Averaging per-microbatch losses or gradients instead of weighting by microbatch size. Equal weight per microbatch overweights small ones.
Stepping the optimizer per microbatch. That trains with the microbatch size while the config claims the global size.
Counting padded or masked positions as batch tokens. Throughput and scaling rules then use tokens the loss never saw.
Zeroing with `zero_grad` defaults that leave stale state. Clear accumulated gradients exactly once per global batch, after the step.

selfTest.q: Microbatch 8 with seq 4096, 4 accumulation steps, dp 2. What is the global batch in samples and tokens?
selfTest.a: \(gbs = 8 \times 4 \times 2 = 64\) samples, or \(64 \times 4096 = 262{,}144\) tokens.

selfTest.q: Why does naive averaging of per-microbatch gradients fail for uneven microbatches?
selfTest.a: Each microbatch gradient is already a mean over its own size. The full-batch mean must weight each by its example count; unweighted averaging gives small microbatches excess influence.

selfTest.q: Does accumulation with the same global batch always match a large batch numerically?
selfTest.a: It matches when every microbatch uses the same graph, the correctly weighted mean, one step per global batch and identical ordering. It differs when padding, dropout draws, batch statistics or ordering differ.

selfTest.q: Where does the extra memory of accumulation sit?
selfTest.a: In gradient buffers held across micro-steps plus one microbatch of activations at a time, instead of the full-batch activation peak.

practice.name: TensorTonic: Gradient Accumulation Equivalence
practice.locator: Implement `gradient_accumulation_step`: accumulate the full-batch mean-squared-error gradient over uneven microbatches and return the updated parameter and full gradient; the public cases check uneven sizes, equal sizes and zero loss
practice.note: Answer the weighting by hand first: each example contributes equally even when microbatch sizes differ. Then run the same comparison in your own trainer against a full-batch step.

units.stopWhen: You derive the global batch in samples and tokens for any setting, and your accumulator matches a full-batch step while the naive mean-of-means fails as predicted.

study.title: Anatomy of a training step
study.locator: ML Frameworks, Anatomy of a Training Step: the seven-statement two-layer MLP traced through forward dispatch, `loss.backward` traversal with `.grad` accumulation and freed saved tensors, and the optimizer update

study.title: Every state object in one file
study.locator: `train_llm.py` model init with `torch.compile`, `DataLoader` with `num_workers=1` and `prefetch_factor=2`, `AdamW(fused=True)`, `CosineAnnealingLR`, the `zero_grad(set_to_none=True)` update block, and the checkpoint block saving model, optimizer and scheduler state dicts

study.title: RNG ownership and deterministic flags
study.locator: `enforce_reproducibility`: torch, CUDA, NumPy and Python RNG streams, `torch.get_rng_state` and `torch.set_rng_state` round trip, and the deterministic-algorithm flags that also belong to the captured state

focus: Parameters and buffers live in the module; gradients accumulate into `.grad` on leaves; optimizer state (momentum, variance, FP32 master copy) lives in the optimizer; scheduler step count lives in the scheduler. Each has exactly one writer per step.

The scaler owns the scale factor and the skip-or-step decision; the RNG streams owned by torch, CUDA, NumPy and Python decide dropout, init and shuffle draws; the loader owns worker processes, prefetch queues and the sampler cursor.
Buffers such as BatchNorm running statistics update by moving average, not by gradient. Forgetting them in a checkpoint corrupts evaluation while training loss looks fine.
`zero_grad(set_to_none=True)` frees gradient storage instead of filling zeros. Reading `.grad` after it without a fresh backward is a use-after-free, not a zero gradient.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw the ownership table for a tiny model with AdamW, cosine schedule, scaler and a two-worker loader: one row per state with owner, dtype, writer and lifetime. Then save and reload every row and show the next-step update matches an uninterrupted run.
traps: Constructing the optimizer before the parameters it should track, or adding new parameters later without extending the optimizer. Those parameters train with no update while the loss still falls.
Saving the model but not the scaler after overflow skips. The resumed run applies a stale scale and overflows again or underflows silently.
Moving the model to a device after building the optimizer. Step kernels then read stale device pointers or silently kept CPU copies.

selfTest.q: Which objects must be saved so an AdamW plus cosine-schedule run resumes its exact trajectory?
selfTest.a: Model, optimizer, scheduler and scaler state dicts plus RNG states and the data position record. Weights alone restart the schedule and the scale history at the wrong point.

selfTest.q: Why do BatchNorm running statistics need checkpointing if they receive no gradients?
selfTest.a: They are updated by forward moving averages and used at evaluation. Restoring weights without them shifts every normalized activation at test time.

selfTest.q: What does `zero_grad(set_to_none=True)` change about `.grad` ownership?
selfTest.a: It releases the gradient tensors so `.grad` becomes None instead of zeros. The next backward reallocates; code that accumulates into `.grad` without checking reads a freed reference.

selfTest.q: A resumed run diverges although model and optimizer were restored. Name two other owners to check first.
selfTest.a: Scheduler position and RNG plus loader position. A shifted schedule or a different example and dropout sequence changes every later update.

units.title: Autograd graphs, backward scheduling, saved tensors and gradient hooks
outcomes: Explain how the backward graph is rebuilt each iteration, which tensors are saved for backward, and when each gradient becomes ready.
Implement a custom autograd `Function` with explicit forward and backward and verify it against a numeric gradient.
Predict hook firing order and which hook side effects break accumulation or overlap.
units.why: Distributed overlap hooks into gradient readiness: a hook that fires late or mutates state delays or corrupts every collective built on top of it. The single-process ordering must be exact first.

next.note: Attach collectives to the readiness order built here.
Trade saved tensors for recompute with open eyes.

study.title: Graph encoding, saved tensors and hook order
study.locator: How autograd encodes the history with Saved tensors (`save_for_backward`, `_saved` attributes, pack and unpack hooks); Backward Hooks execution (whether each of `register_hook`, `register_post_accumulate_grad_hook`, node pre and post hooks fires, and their firing order)

study.title: Differentiation problem and backward cost
study.locator: ML Frameworks, Differentiation Problem: why reverse mode wins for a scalar loss over millions of parameters, the stored-intermediate memory price, and backward at roughly twice forward FLOPs

focus: The graph is rebuilt from scratch every iteration: what you run is what you differentiate. Control flow may change the graph shape each step, so a hook registered on one iteration's node may not exist on the next.

Only operations with at least one input requiring grad are recorded, and only leaves with `requires_grad=True` accumulate `.grad`. A `register_hook` fires while its gradient is computed; a `register_post_accumulate_grad_hook` fires once after accumulation into `.grad`, and only on leaves.

Saved tensors are the forward intermediates backward needs: `x.pow(2)` saves its input for the gradient. Pack hooks run once at save time while unpack hooks may run many times; mutating their inputs in place is forbidden.
In-place operations bump a version counter checked against the saved value at unpack time. A silent wrong gradient cannot pass: misuse raises when `saved_tensors` are accessed.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement a custom autograd `Function` for \(y = x^2\) with `save_for_backward` in forward and the chain-rule product in backward, verify it against a finite-difference gradient, and log the firing order of a tensor hook versus a post-accumulate hook over two steps with accumulation.
traps: Registering a post-accumulate hook on a non-leaf tensor. It errors even with `retain_graph=True`; only leaves accumulate `.grad`.
Mutating a gradient inside a `register_hook` and expecting later hooks to see the original. Hooks compose in order, so each sees the previous hook's output.
Doing collective or CUDA-sync side effects inside a hook during overlap experiments. The hook runs inside backward scheduling, so a blocking call serializes the very overlap being measured.

selfTest.q: Why does `y = x.pow(2)` keep `x` alive after forward?
selfTest.a: Backward needs the input to compute \(2x\). The gradient function saves it at forward time and releases it once backward completes, unless the graph is retained.

selfTest.q: A tensor hook and a post-accumulate hook are registered on the same leaf. Which fires first?
selfTest.a: The tensor hook, while the gradient for that tensor is computed. The post-accumulate hook fires after accumulation into `.grad` finishes at the end of backward.

selfTest.q: Backward is called twice without `retain_graph=True`. What fails and why?
selfTest.a: The second call finds freed saved tensors. The first backward releases intermediates as it traverses unless retention was requested.

selfTest.q: When does a node hook not fire although its tensor received a gradient?
selfTest.a: When the node itself did not execute, for example a tensor passed as `inputs` to `torch.autograd.grad` whose `grad_fn` was skipped. Tensor hooks still fire; node hooks do not.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a custom autograd function or gradient hook with ordering, numerical-result and accumulation-interaction tests against a single-process oracle.
units.stopWhen: Your custom Function matches finite differences, and you can predict for any hook whether it fires, when, and what it observes.

fit.note: Depth failed for hook firing order and saved-tensor packing in the pool books; the official autograd mechanics note fills that gap beside the MLSys differentiation chapter, with implementation practice in the section mini-project.

units.title: FP32, TF32, BF16 and FP16 state, autocast and loss-scaling failures
outcomes: Explain which training state lives in which precision and where accumulation must stay in FP32.
Derive the per-dtype byte counts for parameters, gradients and optimizer state of a small model.
Diagnose lost updates, underflowed gradients and overflowed products from a failing mixed-precision run.
units.why: Precision is a memory and stability contract: the wrong accumulation dtype silently deletes small updates, while the wrong loss scale deletes the gradients. Both look like a healthy run with worse results.

next.note: Turn the byte counts into a full memory ledger.
Trace an overflow back to its first invalid value.

study.title: Mixed Precision Training
study.locator: Sections 1 to 3: FP32 master weights, loss scaling against the FP16 minimum positive normal \(2^{-14}\), and FP32 accumulation; Section 5 for the accuracy-matching evidence across architectures (arXiv:1710.03740v3)

study.title: Dtype states and TF32
study.locator: Tensor Precision with the ML dtype progression; TF32 (`allow_tf32` matmul and cudnn flags); When to use fp32 accumulators (LayerNorm, reductions, gradient accumulation and master weights)

study.title: CS336 Assignment 2: mixed-precision accumulation
study.locator: Section 2.1.5 `mixed_precision_accumulation`: the four-loop `0.01 * 1000` accumulation in fp32 versus fp16; Section 2.1.5 `benchmarking_mixed_precision`: `ToyModel` dtype table under `torch.autocast` and why LayerNorm is sensitive

focus: Three techniques together make FP16 training match FP32: an FP32 master copy updated by the optimizer, a loss scale keeping gradients above the FP16 minimum normal, and FP32 accumulation of products. Each fixes a different failure.

Autocast keeps parameters in FP32 while running matmuls in low precision: a CPU check shows a Linear output in `torch.bfloat16` with `weight.dtype` still FP32. Reductions and norms stay wide because they sum many small terms.
TF32 is a process-global matmul mode, default `allow_tf32` False in the installed build. It changes every matmul silently, so it belongs in the run manifest, not in model code.
The 2018 paper predates BF16 and TF32. Its loss-scaling derivation still holds, but every BF16 range claim must come from the Stas notes or current docs, never from this paper.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, run the four-loop accumulation (`0.01 * 1000` in fp32-on-fp32, fp16-on-fp16, fp32-on-fp16 and cast-back) and explain which loop drifts and why. Then show one overflow fixed by scaling the loss and one small-update loss fixed by FP32 accumulation.
traps: Reading default `GradScaler()` construction as working loss scaling on CPU. It reports enabled but CPU execution keeps it unscaled; real scale dynamics need a CUDA run.
Casting the master weights to FP16 to save memory. Small updates then round to zero and the model freezes while the loss looks algorithmically stuck.
Citing the 2018 paper for BF16 behavior. BF16 has the range of FP32 with short mantissa, the opposite tradeoff to FP16, and the paper predates it.

selfTest.q: FP16 gradients underflow while FP32 loss looks fine. Which of the three techniques is missing or misset?
selfTest.a: Loss scaling. Gradients below the FP16 minimum positive normal flush to zero; scaling the loss up before backward and down after keeps them representable.

selfTest.q: A BF16 run keeps parameters in FP32 under autocast. Why not store them in BF16 directly?
selfTest.a: The optimizer needs the FP32 master copy so small updates accumulate instead of rounding away. Autocast casts to BF16 only for compute.

selfTest.q: Why does LayerNorm stay in FP32 under autocast while linears run narrow?
selfTest.a: It reduces over many elements, so narrow accumulation compounds rounding and its statistics need range. Linears are products plus a single accumulation that the backend keeps wide.

selfTest.q: TF32 was enabled halfway through a study. Which comparisons break?
selfTest.a: All matmul numerics across the flag change. TF32 rounds differently from FP32, so loss, gradient and timing comparisons across the change confound precision with the studied effect.

practice.name: CS336 Assignment 2: `mixed_precision_accumulation` and `benchmarking_mixed_precision`

practice.note: These are writeup problems with no public tests; checking is your own error table plus the dtype table. Run the accumulation loops on CPU, the autocast table needs one GPU.

units.stopWhen: Your accumulation table predicts which loop drifts, and you can attribute a new mixed-precision failure to scale, accumulation width or master-copy dtype.

fit.note: The mixed-precision paper gives the three-technique derivation, the Stas dtype notes add TF32 and BF16 state the paper predates, and the CS336 accumulation problems give named practice.
